title: FlashAttention, slowly: why the IO matters more than the FLOPs
summary: An explainer on FlashAttention. Why standard [[attention]] hits memory bandwidth long before it hits FLOPs, and what the tiling + recomputation trick actually does to fix that.
abstract: Standard [[attention]] over a sequence of length N stores an N×N intermediate matrix, then applies [[softmax]] across rows, then materializes another N×N tensor for the value-weighted sum. On modern GPUs, every one of those reads and writes goes through HBM, and HBM is the bottleneck — not the FLOPs. FlashAttention reorganizes the same exact computation into tiled blocks that fit in SRAM, applies an online softmax across blocks, and recomputes the attention matrix in the backward pass instead of storing it. The result: 2-4× faster attention, longer context windows, identical numerics.
contentIntro:
## Why attention is slow

If you've trained a transformer, you've watched the GPU memory bar fill up faster than the FLOP utilization. That's because [[attention]] is bound by memory bandwidth, not compute. The intermediate `softmax(QK^T/√d_k)` matrix is N×N — for N=8192, that's 67 million floats per head per layer, written to HBM and read back twice.

This explainer walks through the FlashAttention algorithm: tiled blocks that fit in SRAM, online softmax that doesn't need the full row, and recomputation that trades a tiny bit of FLOP for a giant amount of bandwidth. We'll touch [[multi-head-attention]], [[softmax]], and [[backpropagation]] along the way.

## What you should already know

- The attention formula: `softmax(QK^T/√d_k)V`. If `√d_k` is unfamiliar, [[scaling-laws]] is a fine place to start.
- The fact that GPU memory has tiers: registers, SRAM (~megabytes, fast), HBM (~tens of GB, slow).
- That [[backpropagation]] needs to keep cached activations from the forward pass — which is *exactly* the cost FlashAttention is trying to avoid.
contentUndergrad:
## The standard attention forward pass

For a sequence of length N, queries Q ∈ R^{N×d}, keys K ∈ R^{N×d}, values V ∈ R^{N×d}:

1. Compute S = QK^T  (N×N, written to HBM)
2. Compute P = softmax(S/√d_k) row-wise  (N×N, written to HBM)
3. Compute O = PV  (N×d, written to HBM)

Every step is a separate kernel. Every step writes its full output to HBM and reads it back in the next step. The arithmetic intensity is awful: O(Nd) compute per O(N²) memory traffic.

## FlashAttention's three tricks

**(1) Tiling.** Instead of materializing the full S and P matrices, split Q into blocks of B_r rows and K, V into blocks of B_c rows. Each pair (Q_block, K_block) produces a B_r × B_c chunk of attention. We only need one such chunk in SRAM at a time.

**(2) Online softmax.** Computing softmax over a row requires the row's max (for numerical stability) and sum-of-exp. Both are running aggregates: when a new chunk arrives, we update `m_new = max(m_old, m_chunk)`, rescale the running sum by `exp(m_old - m_new)`, and add the chunk's contribution. This means we never need the full row at once — we can stream blocks.

**(3) Recomputation.** Standard backprop caches S and P from the forward pass. FlashAttention skips that: in the backward pass it recomputes S and P from Q, K, V. We pay ~30% extra FLOPs for the recomputation, but we save 2 × N² memory writes — and the GPU is bandwidth-bound, so the wall-clock is faster.

## Why this matters for long contexts

Doubling N quadruples the N² intermediate. At N=32768, the intermediate is over a gigabyte per head per layer. With FlashAttention, the working set scales linearly in N (just Q, K, V), so context windows that were impossible become routine.

Try the [[attention]] page if any of the matrix shapes feel hand-wavy. The [[multi-head-attention]] page covers how this generalizes when you have h parallel heads — the answer: the trick is per-head and embarrassingly parallel.

:::lab[attention-weights-lab]

Play with the lab above to see attention weights on a 6-token sequence. Now imagine that exact computation tiled across blocks: same numerics, vastly less memory.
contentGrad:
## Algorithmic detail

The FlashAttention forward pass, in one block:

```
for j in range(num_kv_blocks):
    K_j = load_kv_block(j)     # SRAM
    V_j = load_kv_block(j)     # SRAM
    for i in range(num_q_blocks):
        Q_i = load_q_block(i)  # SRAM
        S_ij = Q_i @ K_j.T / sqrt(d_k)
        m_ij = rowmax(S_ij)
        P_ij = exp(S_ij - m_ij)
        l_ij = rowsum(P_ij)
        # Update running aggregates for block i
        m_i_new = max(m_i_old, m_ij)
        l_i_new = exp(m_i_old - m_i_new) * l_i_old + exp(m_ij - m_i_new) * l_ij
        O_i = (1 / l_i_new) * (
            exp(m_i_old - m_i_new) * l_i_old * O_i_old
            + exp(m_ij - m_i_new) * P_ij @ V_j
        )
        store_block(O_i, m_i_new, l_i_new)
```

The loop order matters. With q-outer, kv-inner, each Q block is loaded once but each K, V block is loaded N_q times. With kv-outer, q-inner (FlashAttention-2), each K, V is loaded once. The optimization is non-trivial because the running max and sum are per-Q-block, so swapping loop order requires shuffling state.

## Backward pass

FlashAttention's backward recomputes `S` and `P` from Q, K, V using the same tiling. Storing only `(O, l, m)` per row is enough: `(l, m)` lets us reconstruct P, and the chain rule gives ∂L/∂Q, ∂L/∂K, ∂L/∂V via standard matmul. Net memory: O(Nd) instead of O(N²).

## Empirical results

On an A100 with 80 GB HBM and ~40 MB SRAM per SM, FlashAttention-2 sustains 50-70% of theoretical peak FLOPS on attention — vs. 20-30% for standard PyTorch attention. End-to-end, GPT-style training on N=2048 sequences gets ~1.5× wall-clock speedup; at N=8192 the speedup approaches 3×.

## Where it doesn't help

FlashAttention is a memory bandwidth optimization. If you're already compute-bound (very small N, very large d), you'll see less speedup. It also doesn't help with the [[kv-cache]] during inference — that's a different problem (KV-cache reuse, not attention re-computation).

paperStructure.researchQuestion: Can attention be reorganized to be IO-aware on modern GPUs without changing its mathematical output?
paperStructure.method: Tile Q, K, V blocks into SRAM-sized chunks, apply online softmax across blocks, recompute the attention matrix in the backward pass instead of caching it.
paperStructure.results: 2-4× wall-clock speedup on attention, identical numerics, linear memory in sequence length.
